name: DEWINE, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the Ohio Constitution's right to counsel applies only to trials, not preindictment interrogations, and that Morris did not unambiguously invoke his federal Sixth Amendment right to counsel during the interrogation.

name: KENNEDY, C.J.
description: Dissented, argued that while the Ohio Constitution's right to counsel did not attach, the majority improperly addressed the federal Sixth Amendment issue which should have been remanded, and that Morris unambiguously invoked his right to counsel under the Sixth Amendment.

name: LANZINGER, J.
description: Dissented, argued that Morris unambiguously invoked his right to counsel under the Sixth Amendment, and the trial court correctly suppressed statements following this invocation.

name: BRUNNER, J.
description: Dissented, argued that Morris unambiguously invoked his right to counsel under the Sixth Amendment, and the trial court correctly suppressed statements following this invocation.

name: DEWINE, J.
description: Concurred, argued that Ohio's parentage statutes do not apply to unmarried couples, that United States Supreme Court precedent does not empower Ohio courts to retroactively apply the non-spousal artificial insemination statute to unmarried couples, and that the 'would have been married' inquiry is unworkable and at odds with Ohio's rejection of common-law marriage.

name: BRUNNER, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the First District Court of Appeals erroneously decided the case solely on an unpreserved issue and that the Supreme Court should have reversed on that procedural ground without considering the merits.

name: DEWINE, J.
description: Concurred, arguing that the Ohio Constitution's command to pay compensation for taken property applies regardless of whether the property is within the taking municipality's boundaries, thus granting standing for an inverse-condemnation claim.

name: DEWINE, J.
description: Concurred, argued that police officers can be victims under Marsy's Law, and therefore their identifying information in bodycam and dashcam footage is exempt from public disclosure.

name: FISCHER, J.
description: Concurred in part and dissented in part, argued that police officers can be victims under Marsy's Law and their identifying information can be redacted, but the Dispatch is entitled to other limited portions of the requested records.

name: BRUNNER, J.
description: Concurred in part and dissented in part, argued that police officers can be victims, but the Ohio Constitution guarantees the public's right to access government information, requiring unredacted video footage.

name: MENTEL, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the application of the noneconomic damages cap in R.C. 2323.43 to Lyon's catastrophic injuries was unreasonable and arbitrary, violating her due process and equal protection rights, especially when compared to nonmedical tort victims who are not subject to such caps.

name: DEWINE, J.
description: Concurred, argued that Martens lacked standing, expressly overruling the Sheward public-right doctrine as an aberration and finding no taxpayer standing.

name: BRUNNER, J.
description: Concurred in judgment only, arguing that Martens lacked taxpayer standing but that overruling Sheward in this case was procedurally and substantively inappropriate.

name: FISCHER, J.
description: Concurred, argued that R.C. 3705.15 does not permit correcting sex markers based on post-birth changes and that the issue of adversity should have been fully briefed.

name: DONNELLY, J.
description: Concurred, argued that R.C. 3705.15 does not permit corrections to birth records for changes in fact or circumstance after birth, and the legislature should address this gap.

name: BRUNNER, J.
description: Dissented, argued that R.C. 3705.15 authorizes probate courts to correct sex markers and that denying such applications to transgender persons is discriminatory.

name: DETERS, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the judicial power requires adverse interests, and since Adelaide's appeal lacked adversity, the court of appeals had no jurisdiction and should have dismissed the appeal.

name: DEWINE, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the Ohio Constitution's open courts provision requires individualized balancing before sealing juvenile records, making the blanket sealing statute unconstitutional.

name: DONNELLY, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the court should have applied existing balancing tests from prior cases and that the majority's analysis was unnecessarily broad and contained erroneous legal conclusions.

name: STEWART, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the Enquirer did not show a clear legal right to the transcript and that the trial court judge had no legal duty to provide it, and criticized the majority for overturning precedent and announcing a novel interpretation without proper argument from parties.

name: KENNEDY, C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that the same-juror rule applies in all negligence cases where sequential interrogatories separate elements of negligence, requiring the same three-fourths of jurors to concur on all elements for a valid verdict.

name: BRUNNER, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority's application of the same-juror rule to negligence and proximate cause questions upends precedent and erodes the right to a full jury trial, and that the 'any-majority rule' should apply to non-apportionment questions.

name: FISCHER, J.
description: Concurred, arguing that the proposed amendment's mandate for proportional representation constitutes gerrymandering, making the ballot language accurate.

name: DONNELLY, J.
description: Dissented, arguing that the majority's ordered corrections were inadequate and the ballot language remained misleading and argumentative.

name: STEWART, J.
description: Dissented, arguing that the majority's limited corrections were grievously inadequate and the ballot language as a whole was misleading.

name: BRUNNER, J.
description: Dissented, arguing that the ballot board's language was politically biased and required a nearly complete redrafting, which the majority failed to order.

name: DEWINE, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the trial court erred by allowing remote testimony without sufficient case-specific findings of necessity, but this error was harmless given the overwhelming evidence of guilt.

name: FISCHER, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the trial court erred by allowing remote testimony but the error was harmless, and separately argued that the court should revisit its precedent of interpreting the Ohio Constitution's Confrontation Clause in lockstep with the Sixth Amendment.

name: Kennedy, C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that discretionary immunity is a jurisdictional bar, meaning the Court of Claims lacks subject-matter jurisdiction when it applies, and remanded the case to determine if it applies to Ohio State.

name: Brunner, J.
description: Dissented, argued that discretionary immunity is not a jurisdictional bar but an affirmative defense, and the Court of Claims should determine immunity.

name: Donnelly, J.
description: Dissented, argued that discretionary immunity is not a jurisdictional bar but an affirmative defense, and the Court of Claims should determine immunity.

name: Stewart, J.
description: Dissented, argued that discretionary immunity is not a jurisdictional bar but an affirmative defense, and the Court of Claims should determine immunity.

name: DeWine, J.
description: Concurred, argued that Section 29 of H.B. 197 is constitutional and a valid exercise of the General Assembly's authority, as it does not violate the Due Process Clause and the General Assembly has plenary power to enact legislation that does not conflict with state or federal constitutions.

name: Kennedy, C.J.
description: Dissented, argued that Section 29 is unconstitutional because it overrides municipal home-rule authority by compelling municipalities to collect extraterritorial taxes, and that federal due process principles should apply to municipal taxation.

name: Fischer, J.
description: Dissented, argued that Section 29 violates the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment as applied to Schaad, requiring a minimum connection between the taxing authority and the taxed activity.

name: Fischer, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the medical-claim statute of repose clearly and unambiguously includes wrongful-death claims based on medical care, and therefore applies to such claims.

name: Donnelly, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the language of the two statutory schemes (R.C. Chapter 2125 and R.C. 2305.113) does not allow the majority's conclusion and that the General Assembly has not chosen to include wrongful death among the claims listed in R.C. 2305.113(E)(3).

name: Stewart, J.
description: Dissented, concurred in the dissenting opinion of Donnelly, J.

name: Brunner, J.
description: Dissented, argued that applying the medical-malpractice statute of repose to wrongful-death claims unconstitutionally closes the courts to litigants and that these claims are fundamentally different.

name: DEWINE, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the citizens failed to establish that the board acted unlawfully or unreasonably in granting the certificates for the solar farms.

name: BRUNNER, J.
description: Concurred in part and in judgment, argued that the majority opinion improperly discussed agency deference as it was not relevant to the factual determinations of the case.

name: STEWART, J.
description: Concurred, arguing that the majority opinion improperly discussed agency deference as it was not relevant to the factual determinations of the case.

name: DEWINE, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the arson-offender-registration scheme does not violate the separation-of-powers doctrine because the registration duty is not part of the criminal sentence and the legislature has the authority to define criminal sentences and the scope of judicial discretion.

name: STEWART, J.
description: Concurred, argued that while the statute is constitutional, it is problematic due to its lack of guidance for reducing registration periods, which could lead to abuse, arbitrary decisions, and equal-protection issues.

name: BRUNNER, J.
description: Concurred in part and dissented in part, argued that R.C. 2909.15(D)(2)(b) violates the separation-of-powers doctrine by making a judge's discretion to reduce an arson offender's registration period contingent on the executive branch's recommendation, which improperly infringes on judicial power.

name: DONNELLY, J.
description: Concurred in part and dissented in part, argued that R.C. 2909.15(D)(2)(b) violates the separation-of-powers doctrine by allowing the executive branch to control judicial discretion in sentencing.

name: FISCHER, J.
description: Dissented, argued that R.C. 2909.15(D)(2)(b) violates the separation-of-powers doctrine by delegating judicial authority to the executive branch, allowing prosecutors and law enforcement to control a trial court's discretion in sentencing regarding arson registration periods.

name: BRUNNER, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the court should have retained jurisdiction to review the new redistricting plan, as the commission's bipartisan vote does not automatically ensure constitutionality, and the court's prior orders and retained jurisdiction required review.

name: DONNELLY
description: Dissented, argued that the court should have retained jurisdiction to review the new redistricting plan, as the commission's bipartisan vote does not automatically ensure constitutionality, and the court's prior orders and retained jurisdiction required review.

description: Dissented, argued that the court should have retained jurisdiction to review the new redistricting plan, as the commission's bipartisan vote does not automatically ensure constitutionality, and the court's prior orders and retained jurisdiction required review.

name: Fischer, J.
description: Concurred, argued that concurred with majority opinion.

name: Donnelly, J.
description: Concurred, argued that while advocacy seemed to infiltrate the ballot language process, voters would still be fully informed.

name: Stewart, J.
description: Concurred in part and dissented in part, argued that the ballot board failed its constitutional duty by crafting partisan and misleading language, and the full text of the amendment should have been used.

name: Brunner, J.
description: Concurred in part and dissented in part, argued that the ballot board majority shirked its responsibility, obfuscated the amendment's language with deceit and bias, and created misleading language to influence the election outcome, advocating for the full text.

name: Deters, J.
description: Concurred in part and dissented in part, argued that the term "citizens of the State" is not misleading and the ballot language does not deceive voters, disagreeing with the majority's finding on this specific point.

name: Kennedy, C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that concurred with Deters, J.'s opinion.

name: DeWine, J.
description: Concurred, argued that concurred with Deters, J.'s opinion.

name: BRUNNER, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the court should have retained jurisdiction to review the new redistricting plan, as the commission's bipartisan vote does not automatically ensure constitutionality, and the court's prior orders and retained jurisdiction required review.

name: DONNELLY
description: Dissented, argued that the court should have retained jurisdiction to review the new redistricting plan, as the commission's bipartisan vote does not automatically ensure constitutionality, and the court's prior orders and retained jurisdiction required review.

name: STEWART
description: Dissented, argued that the court should have retained jurisdiction to review the new redistricting plan, as the commission's bipartisan vote does not automatically ensure constitutionality, and the court's prior orders and retained jurisdiction required review.

name: Deters, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the Reagan Tokes Law is constitutional as it does not violate the separation-of-powers doctrine, the right to a jury trial, or procedural due process.

name: Brunner, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the Reagan Tokes Law facially violates offenders' rights to procedural due process due to insufficient procedural guarantees and should be invalidated.

name: Donnelly, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the Reagan Tokes Law is unconstitutional due to procedural due process violations.

name: Fischer, J.
description: Concurred in judgment only, agreeing with the outcome but not necessarily all the reasoning.

name: Donnelly, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the General Assembly is bound by its own laws regarding special election dates and cannot use a joint resolution to violate those laws, making the August 8 election unlawful.

name: Stewart
description: Dissented, concurred with Justice Donnelly's opinion, arguing the General Assembly cannot repeal or invalidate statutes by joint resolution.

name: Brunner, J.
description: Dissented, joined Justice Donnelly's opinion and separately argued that the majority's interpretation of "prescribe" is harmful, allowing the General Assembly to violate its own laws and undermining democratic norms.

name: DONNELLY, J.
description: Concurred with the majority's mandated changes but dissented regarding the word "elevating" in the ballot title, arguing it is prejudicial and should be changed to a neutral word.

name: STEWART, J.
description: Concurred in part and dissented in part, joining Judge Donnelly's opinion.

name: BRUNNER, J.
description: Concurred with the majority's mandated changes but dissented, arguing the ballot language should more clearly explain the different standards for citizen-initiated versus General Assembly amendments to avoid obfuscating a fundamental shift in power.

name: Kennedy, C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that the lead opinion improperly adhered to a precedent that grafted a "single-subject rule" onto the people's power to propose constitutional amendments, and that a proposed amendment is not limited to a single subject, object, or purpose.

name: Kennedy, C.J.
description: Concurred in judgment only in part and dissented in part, argued that the majority erred by concluding that judges' oaths of office are governed by the Rules of Superintendence rather than the Public Records Act, and that the court lacks constitutional authority to preempt substantive law.

name: DeWine, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the majority erred by concluding that judges' oaths of office are governed by the Rules of Superintendence rather than the Public Records Act, and that the court lacks constitutional authority to preempt substantive law.

name: O'Connor, C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that the statutory cap on noneconomic damages is unconstitutional as applied to Brandt, violating the due-course-of-law guarantee by arbitrarily excluding severe psychological injuries from exceptions.

name: Kennedy, J.
description: Dissented, arguing that the majority opinion wrongly finds a due-process violation and that the damages caps are constitutional under rational-basis review.

name: Fischer, J.
description: Dissented, arguing that Brandt failed to prove the damages caps are unconstitutional on its face or as applied, and criticized the majority for judicial activism.

name: DeWine, J.
description: Dissented, arguing that the majority opinion wrongly finds a due-process violation and that the damages caps are constitutional under rational-basis review.

name: STEWART, J.
description: Concurred, argued that there is no constitutional right to a jury trial for wrongful imprisonment claims under R.C. 2743.48 because such an action did not exist at common law.

name: KENNEDY, J.
description: Concurred with majority opinion and joined Justice DeWine's concurring opinion.

name: FISCHER, J.
description: Concurred with majority opinion and joined Justice DeWine's concurring opinion.

name: DEWINE, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the jury trial right does not apply due to the lack of a historical analogue and the state's limited waiver of sovereign immunity.

name: DONNELLY, J.
description: Dissented, argued that a constitutional right to a jury trial exists for wrongful imprisonment claims under R.C. 2743.48.

name: BRUNNER, J.
description: Dissented with majority opinion and joined Justice Donnelly's dissenting opinion.

name: BRUNNER
description: Concurred, argued that victims had a right to restitution under Marsy's Law but forfeited it by not appealing the initial denial, and the trial court lost jurisdiction after the sentence became final.

name: O'Connor
description: Concurred, argued that the trial court lacked jurisdiction to modify Brasher's sentence solely because the Double Jeopardy Clause prohibited imposing restitution after the sentence was completed.

name: DeWine
description: Concurred, argued that the trial court erred for two independent reasons: lack of jurisdiction after final judgment and expired appeal time, and violation of Double Jeopardy due to Brasher's legitimate expectation of finality.

name: Stewart, J.
description: Concurred, argued that Morris's life sentence without considering his youth as a mitigating factor constitutes cruel and unusual punishment under both Ohio and federal constitutions, consistent with *State v. Patrick*.

name: FISCHER, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority incorrectly reaffirms *State v. Patrick* which was overruled by *Jones v. Mississippi* on federal law, and that the Ohio Constitution does not independently require on-the-record consideration of youth.

name: KENNEDY
description: Dissented, argued that while youth must be considered, the Eighth Amendment does not require courts to expressly consider a juvenile's age on the record, and *State v. Patrick* should be overruled on that point.

name: DeWINE, J.
description: Dissented, argued that while youth must be considered, the Eighth Amendment does not require courts to expressly consider a juvenile's age on the record, and *State v. Patrick* should be overruled on that point.

name: Brunner, J.
description: Concurred, argued that R.C. 2152.84(A)(2)(b) is fundamentally unfair as applied to D.R. because it removes judicial discretion at a critical stage, violating due process.

name: Fischer, J.
description: Dissented, argued that R.C. 2152.84 complies with due process because no existing protected substantive right is at stake at the completion-of-disposition stage.

name: DeWine, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority misinterprets procedural due process and that the law requiring sex offender registration for 16- and 17-year-olds is constitutional.

name: Kennedy, J.
description: Concurred with Justice DeWine's dissenting opinion.

name: Brunner, J.
description: Concurred, argued that a criminal defendant has a constitutional and statutory right to a bill of particulars upon request, which the state must provide and cannot substitute with open-file discovery.

name: DeWine, J.
description: Dissented, argued that Haynes forfeited his argument by changing it on appeal and suffered no prejudice as all information was in discovery.

name: Kennedy, J.
description: Dissented, argued that Haynes failed to raise the argument below and the Sixth District Court of Appeals' judgment should be affirmed.

name: Brunner, J.
description: Concurred, argued that Marsy's Law provides a right to "full and timely restitution" but did not alter the meaning of "restitution" in Ohio law, which is limited to economic losses directly and proximately caused by the offense, thus excluding lost wages for court attendance.

name: DeWine, J.
description: Dissented, argued that Ohio voters approved Marsy's Law to significantly expand victims' rights, including the right to "full and timely restitution," and that lost wages due to court attendance are a foreseeable consequence of the crime and should be compensable.

name: KENNEDY, J.
description: Concurred, but only in the judgment.

name: FISCHER, J.
description: Concurred, but only in the judgment.

name: DEWINE, J.
description: Concurred, but only in the judgment.

name: Donnelly, J.
description: Concurred in denying the motion to strike, denying attorney fees, and denying placement on the November 8 ballot, but dissented from granting the writ of mandamus ordering the Sandusky City Commission to enact an ordinance for submission to electors.

name: Brunner, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the precedent in Hackworth was correctly decided, meaning R.C. 731.31 should apply to charter amendment petitions, and therefore the writ of mandamus should have been denied in full.

name: Brunner, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the March 2 plan is not lawful, the record does not support the dissent's claim of maximizing competitive seats, and the respondents' abuse of legislative privilege is unjustifiable.

name: Kennedy, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the March 2 plan is constitutional because it does not excessively split counties and reasonably attempts to maximize competitive seats, and the majority's analysis relies on an unconstitutional proportionality standard.

name: DeWine, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the March 2 plan is constitutional because it does not excessively split counties and reasonably attempts to maximize competitive seats, and the majority's analysis relies on an unconstitutional proportionality standard.

name: Fischer, J.
description: Dissented, argued that petitioners failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the March 2 plan unduly favors the Republican Party, and criticized the court's compressed schedule and lack of transparency.

name: Kennedy, J.
description: Dissented, argued that neither group of relators had a clear legal right to relief as the federal court order did not extend filing deadlines, and the majority's decision was an exercise of raw political power that disrupted the election process.

name: Fischer, J.
description: Dissented, argued that neither group of relators had a clear legal right to relief, joining Justice Kennedy's opinion and emphasizing the chaos caused by the court's redistricting decisions.

name: DeWine, J.
description: Dissented, argued that neither the court nor the Secretary of State had authority to alter legislative filing deadlines, and the federal court order did not implicitly move these deadlines, leading to disruption and unconstitutional action.

name: Kennedy, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the Ohio Constitution grants the General Assembly spending power and authority to establish courts, and the challenged statutes do not invade municipal home-rule powers.

name: Fischer, J.
description: Concurred, argued that Ohio's jurisprudence on standby and hybrid representation needs reevaluation, as current guidelines create impossible situations for standby counsel and hybrid representation is constitutionally supported by the Ohio Constitution's text.

name: BRUNNER, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the transfer restriction is valid, reasonable, and serves a charitable or public purpose, and that the state is entitled to relief as contemplated in the agreement.

name: Donnelly, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the CDC violated enforceable land-transfer restrictions and OPWC was entitled to seek remedies, but did not join the part of the opinion discussing the enforceability of use restrictions on surface or subsurface property as that issue was not raised by the parties.

name: DeWine, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the transfer restriction is an invalid and unreasonable restraint on alienation under both traditional common law and modern reasonableness tests, and the court should have reinstated the trial court's judgment.

name: Kennedy, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the transfer restriction is an invalid and unreasonable restraint on alienation.

name: Fischer, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the transfer restriction is an invalid and unreasonable restraint on alienation.

name: Donnelly, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the enacted congressional-district plan is an unconstitutional partisan gerrymander that unduly favors the Republican Party and splits governmental units.

name: Brunner, J.
description: Concurred, joining the majority opinion and Chief Justice O'Connor's concurring opinion.

name: O'Connor, C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that the evidence overwhelmingly shows the map creates an undue partisan advantage for the Republican Party, and that "competitiveness" is not a valid constitutional standard.

name: Kennedy, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority's decision lacks a workable legal standard for "undue" favoritism or splitting and improperly substitutes policy preferences for the law.

name: Fischer, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority's decision lacks a workable legal standard for "undue" favoritism or splitting and improperly substitutes policy preferences for the law.

name: DeWine, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority's decision lacks a workable legal standard for "undue" favoritism or splitting and improperly substitutes policy preferences for the law.

name: Donnelly, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the trial court's bail was set at an unaffordable level, and denying bail requires specific statutory procedures, not excessive bail.

name: Kennedy, J.
description: Dissented, argued that DuBose did not prove the trial court abused its discretion in setting bail, which was valid given the serious charges, flight risk, and threat to the victim's family.

name: Fischer, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the abuse-of-discretion standard of review is appropriate for excessive bail petitions when no new evidence is presented.

name: DeWine, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority's decision undermines public safety, victim rights, and trial court discretion in setting bail.

name: Stewart, J.
description: Concurred, argued that a municipality can acquire excess electricity for reasons other than solely reselling it extraterritorially, but not solely for that purpose, and material facts remain.

name: DeWine, J.
description: Concurred in part and dissented in part, argued that a municipality lacks constitutional authority to resell purchased electricity to those outside its limits, as Sections 4 and 6 only permit selling surplus product that the municipality produced itself.

name: Fischer, J.
description: Concurred with Justice DeWine's opinion, arguing that a municipality lacks constitutional authority to resell purchased electricity to those outside its limits, as Sections 4 and 6 only permit selling surplus product that the municipality produced itself.

name: Kennedy, J.
description: Dissented, argued that Article XVIII, Section 6 expressly authorizes municipalities to sell excess electricity to nonresidents, and the Constitution does not prohibit selling an "artificial" surplus, and Toledo Edison Co. should be overruled.

name: Brunner, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the lead opinion misapplies Toledo Edison Co. and that Cleveland Electric failed to meet its burden for summary judgment, so summary judgment should have been granted for the city.

name: O'Connor, C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that Judge Peeler's order restoring federal firearms rights to Ewing was unauthorized by law and that Suwalski, as a victim, had no other adequate remedy to challenge the erroneous order under Marsy's Law.

name: Kennedy, J.
description: Dissented, argued that Marsy's Law rights asserted by Suwalski were not implicated in the relief-from-disability matter because Ewing was no longer 'the accused' and Suwalski lacked standing to bring the prohibition action.

name: O'Connor, C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that a warrantless public arrest based on probable cause is constitutional and does not require exigent circumstances or impracticability of obtaining a warrant.

name: Stewart, J.
description: Dissented, argued that law enforcement officers acted outside their statutory authority by making a warrantless arrest when they had ample time to secure a warrant, violating Article I, Section 14 of the Ohio Constitution.

name: Brunner, J.
description: Dissented, argued that law enforcement officers acted outside their statutory authority by making a warrantless arrest when they had ample time to secure a warrant, violating Article I, Section 14 of the Ohio Constitution.

name: KENNEDY, J.
description: Concurred, argued that Sierah's Law is remedial and its retroactive application does not violate the Ohio Constitution's Retroactivity Clause.

name: STEWART, J.
description: Dissented, argued that Sierah's Law is punitive and its retroactive application violates the Ohio Constitution's Retroactivity Clause.

name: DONNELLY, J.
description: Dissented, argued that Sierah's Law is punitive and its retroactive application violates the Ohio Constitution's Retroactivity Clause.

name: BRUNNER, J.
description: Dissented, argued that Sierah's Law is punitive and its retroactive application violates the Ohio Constitution's Retroactivity Clause.
